title: DHS Publishes Rule to End 60-Day Grace Period for Laid-Off H-1B Workers
excerpt: The proposed regulation, published in the Federal Register on September 11, would strip the safety net that has let foreign workers stay in the US for up to 60 days after a layoff — and is open for public comment through November 10.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security published a formal proposal on September 11, 2026, to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN, E-1, E-2, E-3 and H-1B1 workers whose employment ends — and their dependents.
  • If finalized, a laid-off worker would fall out of status the day after their job ends and be expected to leave the US immediately, unless they have another authorized basis to stay.
  • Indian nationals, who received 72.3% of H-1B approvals in fiscal year 2024, are by far the largest group affected. DHS itself estimates roughly 3,795 workers a year could face lost income from a forced, immediate departure.
  • The public comment period is open through November 10, 2026, via regulations.gov under Docket USCIS-2026-0364. The rule cannot take effect until comments are reviewed and a final rule is issued.

The proposal

The Trump administration has proposed eliminating a 60-day grace period that allows foreign workers on H-1B and certain other temporary visas to remain in the United States and find a new sponsor after losing their jobs, according to a notice published in the Federal Register on September 11, 2026. The proposal, titled "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-day Grace Period," is Docket USCIS-2026-0364, published at 91 FR 57807, and targets regulation 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) for removal in its entirety.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=KFnjQltLYTA

Under the planned rule change, workers in H-1B, H-1B1, E-1, E-2, E-3, L-1, O-1 and TN status — along with their dependent spouses and children — would have to leave the country as soon as their qualifying employment ends. A worker whose last day of pay arrives without a new employer petition already filed would fall out of status the following day.

Why the grace period existed

The 60-day grace period dates to a 2016 Obama-era regulation known as the AC21 retention rule, which took effect on January 17, 2017. It gave high-skilled workers up to 60 consecutive days — or the remainder of their authorized stay, if shorter — to find a new sponsor, file a change-of-status petition, or arrange an orderly departure after a layoff.

The window became the standard safety net through the waves of tech layoffs beginning in 2022, giving workers time to arrange new sponsorship, sell property, and pull children out of school rather than facing same-day departure. It was never a guarantee — immigration officers could shorten it case by case — but in practice it functioned as the buffer between a pink slip and a plane ticket.

What DHS says

The department argues the grace period has "disconnected" a foreign national's status from the basis on which it was granted and is too costly to administer. In the proposal's justification, DHS says its officers had to evaluate the application of the grace period in more than 1.9 million applications and petitions between October 2017 and May 2026.

"This proposal restores a direct relationship between an alien's nonimmigrant status and the specific employment or activity that formed the basis of his or her admission or grant of status in the United States."

— US Department of Homeland Security, Federal Register notice

DHS wrote that companies disrupted by the change could see the jobs go to American workers instead. "DHS presumes that they will either offer the same jobs to equally qualified U.S. workers or go through the I-129 petition process depending on their workforce requirement," the notice said, according to Reuters.

The human cost, in DHS's own numbers

The agency acknowledges the rule would create real hardship. Its regulatory-impact analysis says affected workers could face airfare and transportation costs, lease-termination fees, time arranging a sudden departure, and lost income. DHS's own estimate puts the number of nonimmigrant beneficiaries who could face lost income from a forced, immediate departure at roughly 3,795 per year.

Immigration law firm Fragomen warned that workers who fall out of status under the new regime could be issued Notices to Appear — the government's first step in initiating removal, or deportation, proceedings. Dependents, including spouses and children in H-4 and related statuses, would lose the ability to remain in the US if the principal worker's grace-period eligibility ends.

What it means for Indian workers

Indian nationals are the single largest exposed cohort. They received 72.3% of H-1B approvals in USCIS fiscal year 2024, making them disproportionately affected by any change to H-1B employment rules. The grace-period proposal follows a string of Trump administration moves limiting legal migration since January 2025, including higher visa fees for skilled workers and a pause on immigrant visa appointments at US missions abroad while a new training program is implemented, according to Reuters.

For a laid-off Indian tech worker in the Bay Area or Seattle, the practical difference is stark: under current rules, there are up to 60 days to line up a new H-1B transfer, change to a dependent or visitor status, or depart. Under the proposal, those arrangements would need to be filed and receipted before the last day of pay — or the worker would need to leave the United States and complete visa processing abroad before returning.

What happens next

The rule is not yet in force. The proposal entered a 60-day public comment period when published on September 11, with comments due November 10, 2026, filed through the Federal eRulemaking Portal at regulations.gov under Docket USCIS-2026-0364. DHS must review comments before it can issue a final rule, a process that typically takes months — and final rules are frequently challenged in court.

The White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs completed its review of the measure at the end of August 2026, clearing it for publication. Employers, immigration attorneys, and affected workers are expected to file extensive comments during the window. For now, the 60-day grace period remains the law.
